t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.1.ref: Lines 14–25 and 129–164 (the seven attributes and the seven gates)
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.1.texto: Paraphrase. Inanna takes the seven me and holds them in her hand. She puts on her head the šugurra crown, "turban of the steppe"; she places a lock of hair on her forehead; she takes in her hand the lapis lazuli measuring rod and line; she puts small lapis lazuli beads around her neck and twin egg-shaped beads on her breast; she covers herself with the pala robe, the garment of ladyship; she paints her eyes with the kohl called "let a man come, let him come"; she puts on the pectoral called "come, man, come" and a gold ring on her hand. At each of the seven gates the gatekeeper takes one of these things from her. She asks: "What is this?". They answer her: "Be silent, Inanna, the rites of the Underworld are perfect. Inanna, do not open your mouth against the rites of the Underworld". At the last gate they take off her robe, and she enters naked and bowed down.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.1.fuent: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.4.1 and Sladek (1974)
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.1.nota_: The order of the objects varies between copies. They are at once jewelry, clothing and emblems of power: the measuring rod and line are attributes of kingship and of justice (they appear on the stele of Ur-Namma). The names of the kohl and the pectoral allude to sexual attraction, one of Inanna's spheres. The progressive stripping reverses the royal investiture and prepares her death: in the Underworld no one keeps their distinctions.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.1.lectu: Sitchin interprets Inanna's attributes (the headdress, the "twin beads" on her breast, the rod and the line) as flight equipment: helmet, earphones, navigation instruments. To support this he makes comparisons with figures wearing a helmet or goggles, such as the statue of the "goddess with the flowing vase" from Mari, which he presents as Inanna in a pilot's suit.

The poem names and describes the objects: a crown or turban, a hairstyle, lapis lazuli necklaces, a garment, kohl, a pectoral, a ring, the surveyor's rod and line. All of them are documented in art and in temple inventories. The Mari statue (c. 1800 BC) is a water goddess with a horned tiara and a vase from which water flows; her "goggles" are the large inlaid eyes usual in Mesopotamian sculpture.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.2.texto: Paraphrase. Inanna makes her sister rise from the throne and sits on it. The Anunna, the seven judges, deliberate before her. They look at her: it is the look of death. They speak to her: it is the word of wrath. They shout at her: it is the shout of guilt. The afflicted woman is turned into a corpse, and the corpse is hung on a hook. After three days have passed, Ninshubur weeps for her before Enlil and Nanna, who turn her away, saying that whoever craves the rites of the Underworld must stay there. Enki is grieved, takes the dirt from under his fingernails and creates the kurgarra; from the dirt of another fingernail he creates the gala-tura. He gives them the food and water of life. They slip in like flies through the cracks of the doors and find Ereshkigal, the mother who gives birth, lying down, naked and in pain. When she groans "Oh, my inside!", they groan "Oh, your inside!"; when she groans "Oh, my outside!", they repeat it. Grateful, she offers them the river full of water and the field full of grain, but they ask only for "the corpse that hangs on the hook". They sprinkle it with the food and water of life, and Inanna rises.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.2.fuent: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.4.1 and Sladek (1974)
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.2.nota_: The kurgarra and the gala are figures of Inanna's cult, ritual personnel with an ambiguous gender identity; the gala was the singer of laments. That Enki creates them from the dirt under his fingernails underlines his ingenuity in the face of Enlil's law. The scene of shared laments is an early example of the ritual efficacy of empathy. The myth does not say why Ereshkigal is suffering: some readings suggest childbirth or grief for her husband.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.2.lectu: The version by Diane Wolkstein and Samuel Noah Kramer turned the hymns and myths of Inanna into a cult book for the goddess spirituality movement. It presents the descent as the journey of a powerful woman into the depths of herself, and it was adapted for theater and music.
Diane Wolkstein and Samuel Noah Kramer, Inanna, Queen of Heaven and Earth: Her Stories and Hymns from Sumer, 1983
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.3.texto: Paraphrase. Inanna ascends surrounded by galla demons, who know neither food nor drink, accept no offerings, and tear the wife from her husband's lap and the child from the wet nurse's breast. Ninshubur throws herself at her feet dressed in sackcloth, and Inanna refuses to hand her over. Nor does she hand over Shara of Umma or Lulal of Bad-tibira, who await her in mourning. In Kulaba, under the great apple tree, Dumuzi sits on his throne, dressed in a magnificent robe. Inanna looks at him with the look of death and says: "Take him away!". Dumuzi weeps and asks Utu, his brother-in-law, to turn him into a snake so that he can escape; Utu helps him, but the demons catch him. At the end of the poem, Inanna decrees that Dumuzi will spend half the year in the Underworld and his sister Geshtinanna the other half. The poem concludes with praise of Ereshkigal.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.3.fuent: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.4.1 and Sladek (1974); the ending is completed with "The Death of Dumuzi" and other texts
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.3.nota_: The old reading (Frazer, Langdon) that made Dumuzi a god who dies and rises again every year was qualified when Kramer published the end of the poem in the 1950s: Inanna does not go down to rescue him but hands him over. The alternation with Geshtinanna has been related to agricultural cycles (grain and the vine) or pastoral ones, but the text does not make it explicit.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.4.ref: Akkadian version: The Descent of Ishtar, lines 1–20
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.4.fuent: Spanish version based on R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (1912), pp. 121–122, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.4.nota_: The Akkadian version is not a translation of the Sumerian one but a short reworking, perhaps linked to funerary rites and to laments for Dumuzi (Tammuz). In line 19 Rogers doubted his own translation ("they will raise up the dead, who will eat the living"), but today it is accepted (Lapinkivi 2010). The description of the Underworld (dust and clay as food, the dead clothed in feathers) is repeated almost identically in Enkidu's dream in Gilgamesh VII. Ishtar appears here as the daughter of Sin (the Moon god), the Akkadian equivalent of Nanna.
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.version: Sumerian poem of about 280 lines, known from Old Babylonian copies from Nippur (the main one in the Penn Museum) and one from Ur with variants
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.estructura.0.sin: Praise of Dilmun, a pure and virgin land where there is still no illness or old age, nor animals that kill; but there is no fresh water either. At Ninsikila's request, Enki makes water spring forth and Dilmun becomes a port and trading center.
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.estructura.1.sin: Enki impregnates Ninhursag (Nintur), who after nine days gives birth to Ninnisig; Enki lies with his daughter, who bears Ninkura; and from her Uttu, the goddess of weaving, is born. Ninhursag advises Uttu to demand gifts of fruit; Enki seduces her with them, and from the semen that Ninhursag collects from Uttu's body eight plants spring up.
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.estructura.2.sin: Enki, guided by his vizier Isimud, tastes and eats the eight plants, "knowing their heart" and determining their destiny. Ninhursag curses him and withdraws; Enki falls ill in eight parts of his body. A fox manages to bring Ninhursag back.
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.estructura.3.sin: Ninhursag seats Enki in her vulva and gives birth to eight deities, one for each ailing part, who are assigned destinies and functions. Final praise of Enki.
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.pasajes.0.texto: Paraphrase. "Pure is the land of Dilmun". It is a clean, bright and virgin land, where the raven does not croak, the lion does not kill, the wolf does not snatch the lamb, no one says "my eyes hurt" or "my head hurts", no old woman says "I am old". […] After eating the plants born of his own semen, Enki is cursed by Ninhursag, who swears never again to look at him "with the eye of life" until he dies, and disappears. The gods sit down in the dust. A fox offers Enlil to bring her back in exchange for a reward, grooms itself and finds her. Ninhursag returns and asks Enki: "Brother, what hurts you?". "The top of my head hurts": and she gives birth to Abu. "My hair hurts": Nintulla is born. "My nose hurts": Ninsutu is born. "My mouth hurts": Ninkasi, the goddess of beer, is born. "My throat hurts": Nanshe is born. "My arm hurts": Azimua is born. "My ribs (ti) hurt": Ninti, "lady of the rib", is born. "My side hurts": Enshag is born, who will be lord of Dilmun.
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.pasajes.0.fuente: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.1.1 and Attinger (1984); "Pure is the land of Dilmun" is a short quotation translated from ETCSL 1.1.1, line 1
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.pasajes.0.nota_a: Dilmun is the island of Bahrain and the neighboring coast of the Persian Gulf, a center of trade with Mesopotamia. Kramer (1945) read Dilmun as a "paradise" comparable to Eden and linked Ninti, "lady of the rib" and also "lady who gives life" (ti means both in Sumerian), with Eve, formed from a rib and called "mother of all living". The parallel is still debated, but it points to a real play on words. Today there is a tendency to read the opening not as a paradise but as a world not yet set in motion. The births associated with each part of the body are etiological puns.
t.textos.enki-ninhursag.pasajes.0.lectur: Sitchin presents Ninhursag as the "chief medical officer" of the Anunnaki and Enki as a scientist. Enki's successive unions with his descendants would be genetic experiments to obtain an heir, and the healing of the organs an advanced medical practice.

The text is a myth of fertility and origins written with puns: each goddess is born to heal a part of the body whose name sounds like hers. Ninhursag is the mother goddess, venerated as "mother of the gods", not a scientific post. The sequence of unions repeats ritual formulas and has no biological content.

Feminist readings stress that the myth narrates a god's successive abuses of his daughter, granddaughter and great-granddaughter, and the response of the mother goddess, who turns the violence into the god's illness and then heals him by giving birth: the goddess keeps power over life and generation.
Tikva Frymer-Kensky, In the Wake of the Goddesses, 1992
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.version: Sumerian poem of about 470 lines, known from Old Babylonian copies from Nippur and Ur
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.estructura.0.s: Praise of Enki as lord of the Apsu, of wisdom and of fertility, who fixes the destinies of the lands and counts the days and the months.
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.estructura.1.s: Enki twice proclaims his greatness and the trust that An and Enlil have given him; the gods and the priests of the Apsu answer him with praises.
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.estructura.2.s: Journey and destinies of the lands (lines 140–249)
Enki travels the world in his boat and decrees the destiny of Sumer, Ur, Meluhha (the Indus Valley), Dilmun, Elam and Marhashi, and of the nomadic peoples.
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.estructura.3.s: Enki fills the Tigris with living water, like his semen, organizes canals, marshes, sea, rain, fields, plow, grain, bricks, building, steppe, herds, boundaries and weaving, and entrusts each sphere to a deity.
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.estructura.4.s: Inanna protests because she has not received any function like her divine sisters. Enki reminds her of the powers she already has (war, the shepherd's crook, speech, ambiguity) and praises her.
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.pasajes.0.text: Paraphrase. Enki rises like a bull and fills the Tigris with sparkling water, like semen. The Tigris rejoices like a wild bull and yields grain and wine. Enki entrusts the canals to Enbilulu, the inspector of canals. He organizes the reed beds and the fish of the marsh, and hands the sea over to Nanshe. He calls the rain and sets Ishkur over it. He directs the plow and the yoke, opens the furrows and hands these things over to Enkimdu, the farmer; he makes the grain grow and entrusts it to Ezina-Ashnan. He fixes the brick mold and the hoe for Kulla; he lays the foundations and the plumb line for Mushdama, the builder. He fills the steppe with animal life and hands it over to Shakkan. He builds the sheepfolds and places the shepherd Dumuzi in charge. He fixes the boundaries and entrusts them to Utu. He entrusts weaving, the work of women, to Uttu.
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.pasajes.0.fuen: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.1.3 and Benito (1969)
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.pasajes.0.nota: It is the great Sumerian text on the distribution of the divine functions (me) and a kind of encyclopedia of the economy of Sumer: irrigation, fishing, agriculture, building, herding, crafts. Fresh water is presented at the same time as Enki's semen, a sexual metaphor for agricultural fertility frequent in Sumerian literature. The list of lands (Meluhha, Magan, Dilmun) reflects the real trade networks of the 3rd millennium.
t.textos.enki-orden-mundo.pasajes.0.lect: The poem is read today as a vision of the world in which nature is already organized for human labor: the river, the steppe and the marsh make sense only when a god assigns them administrators. It is an ideal of managed landscape typical of an irrigation civilization.
Synthesis of ecocritical readings; see also Thorkild Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness, 1976
